Purpose: A name that can be used in the scene tree and in a running game to find items.
The x, y, and z coordinates of the item. In 2D, the z coordinate says whether an item is in front of or behind another.
How large the item is along x, y, and, in 3D, z. A scale of 1 is the item's normal size.
In 2D, one angle twists the image. In 3D, the item can be turned by its yaw (left and right), pitch (up and down), and roll (tilting to the side).
In 3D, the item's red, green, and blue amounts, each from 0 to 1.
If this is checked, the item takes part in physics.
The item is taken into account for collisions, but physics never moves it. A wall is a good example.
The item can be moved, but does not respond to physical forces. An example would be a moving platform.
The item responds to physical forces like gravity, force, and torque. Choosing it gives the item a mass of 1 if its mass was 0.
The mass of the item, measured in kilograms. Heavier items are harder to push.
How much friction the item has. 0 means it slides like ice; larger numbers make it grip.
How bouncy the item is. A value of 0 does not bounce, whereas 1 means it bounces back to its original height. A number above 1 bounces higher than where it started.
